content:
Popular writing on Islamic end times mixes three layers: what the Quran says, what the hadith (the reports of the words and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him) add, and what later tradition built on top. Most of the confusion comes from treating them as one.

Each of the five entries below is placed in its layer. Some beliefs rest on the Quran, some on hadith that both major collections record, and some on reports that scholars have graded differently. A Muslim is bound to the first group, may weigh the others, and is never given a calendar.

"They ask you about the Hour: when will it come? Say, its knowledge is with my Lord alone."[1] That is the Quran's position, and the Prophet repeated it. When Gabriel asked him about the Hour he answered, "The one asked knows no more than the one asking."[2] A man once asked him when the Hour would come, and he replied with a question: what have you prepared for it?[3]

The man's answer, in the version recorded by al-Bukhari, was that he had not prepared much prayer or fasting or charity, but that he loved God and His Messenger. The Prophet told him: "You will be with those you love." Anas, who narrated it, said that nothing had made the Companions happier.[4] The exchange shows where the Prophet turned the question of the end: away from the calendar and towards the state of the person asking.

This is the first test of any claim about dates. A prediction that the end will come in a given year contradicts the Quran. A critic may reply that the Prophet is also reported to have said that he and the Hour were sent like two fingers held side by side.[5] The hadith expresses nearness, and nearness has no number attached to it. Fourteen centuries have passed since he spoke, and the Quran itself says that a day with God may be as a thousand years of human counting.

The hadith do list signs, and they come in two kinds. The minor signs are social: people competing in building tall buildings, a loss of trust, a spread of ignorance.[6] The Prophet said that when trust is lost, one should wait for the Hour, and that knowledge would be taken away as the scholars die.[7] The major signs are ten, among them the Dajjal, the return of Jesus, Gog and Magog, and the sun rising from the west.[8]

Two of the ten also appear in the Quran: Gog and Magog, and the beast that speaks to people. The sunrise from the west is tied to the verse that says faith will profit no soul on the day some of the Lord's signs arrive.[9] Scholars separate the signs that have already appeared from those still to come, and they warn against pointing at a current event and calling it the final sign. Every generation has done so, and the signs have been wrongly claimed many times.

The signs are warnings to live carefully. The Prophet is not reported to have given them as a means of working out the date.

The return of Jesus is the major sign Muslims know best. The Quran says that he is a sign of the Hour and that every one of the People of the Book will believe in him before his death, which most commentators read as a reference to his return.[10] The Prophet said that Jesus son of Mary would descend as a just judge, break the cross, kill the swine and abolish the jizya, and that wealth would become so abundant that no one would accept it.[11] Muslims expect him as a follower of the Prophet's law, ending the disputes about himself.

The reports about Gog and Magog have a striking image. Zaynab bint Jahsh said that the Prophet once woke with a red face, saying that a gap had opened in the barrier of Gog and Magog, and making a circle with his fingers to show its size.[12] The commentators read it as a warning that the trials of the end had begun to move, which is a statement of moral urgency, and they did not take it as a date.

The Dajjal, "the deceiver", is not named in the Quran. He comes from the hadith, which describe a false claimant who is blind in one eye and who will tempt people with wonders.[13] The Prophet said that every prophet warned his people about him.[14] A critic can fairly ask why a figure so grave is missing from the Quran. The answer is that the Quran leaves many matters to the Prophet's explanation, as it does with the number and form of the daily prayers, and the reports about the Dajjal come through many Companions in both major collections.

The detail Muslims are taught is the test. His wonders are real, and the answer to him is faith and a recitation of the opening verses of Surah al-Kahf.[15] Muslims are also taught to seek refuge from his trial at the end of every prayer.[16] The figure stands for the final trial of belief against appearance.

Muslim scholars drew a lesson for every age from the reports. The Dajjal deceives by wonders and by offering prosperity to those who follow him, and the believer resists by holding to what God has revealed. Many writers have seen in the description a pattern that recurs whenever a power demands loyalty by appealing to appearances. The reports themselves describe a person, and the scholars warned against naming him in advance.

Many Muslims expect a just leader from the Prophet's family before the end. The Quran does not mention the Mahdi. The reports come from hadith collections, in particular Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, and scholars have graded them differently.[17] One report says that if only a day of the world remained, God would lengthen it until He sent a man from the Prophet's family. Neither al-Bukhari nor Muslim includes the Mahdi reports under that name. Some great scholars, among them Ibn Khaldun, who examined the chains in his Muqaddimah, doubted them.[18] Others, including Ibn Taymiyya, accepted that the reports are sound taken together.[19]

So this is the one item on the list that a Muslim can reject or accept without leaving the faith. Belief in the Last Day is required. Belief in the Mahdi is a matter of the scholars' judgement of the reports. History adds a caution: men who claimed the title, in the Sudan in the 1880s and at Mecca in 1979, were opposed by the great majority of Muslim scholars.

Twelver Shia Muslims hold a more definite belief. They identify the Mahdi with the twelfth imam, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, who they believe went into hiding in the ninth century and will return.[20] That doctrine is central to Twelver faith and has shaped Shia thought and politics for a thousand years. Sunni scholars have not accepted the identification, while many of them accept that a Mahdi from the Prophet's family will appear.

"Who is there that can intercede with Him except by His permission?"[21] The Quran limits intercession at the root: nobody can plead with God unless God allows it, and then only for those He is pleased with.[22] Other verses say that on the Day of Judgement no intercession will benefit those who deny it, which critics read as a contradiction of the hadith below.[23] The verses address two different things. One denies intercession as of right, and the other grants it by permission.

Within that limit, the Prophet said that on the Day of Judgement people will go to the prophets one by one asking for help, and each will excuse himself until they come to Muhammad, who will prostrate before God and then be told to ask.[24] Most commentators take the "praised station" promised to him in the Quran to refer to this.[24] The Mu'tazila denied that intercession could lift a grave sinner out of punishment, and the Sunni schools affirmed it. It is a picture of mercy delivered by permission and not by right.

The Quran's picture of the Day itself is one of exact justice. It speaks of the scales set up so that no soul is wronged in the least, and says that whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.[25] Intercession works within that justice. It is a gift of mercy granted by God, and it does not set the scales aside.

The bottom line

The evidence sorts itself by strength. The certainty that the Hour will come and that no creature knows its time rests on the Quran. The signs, the Dajjal and the return of Jesus rest on hadith that are widely transmitted, and Muslims accept them as part of the faith. The Mahdi and the details of order rest on reports that scholars have weighed differently, and Muslims may differ there without blame.

Anyone who offers a date, or who names a living person as the Dajjal or the Mahdi, claims more than the sources give. The sources give a warning and a way to prepare: faith, care in conduct and trust in God's mercy.

The Prophet put the right attitude into a single instruction: if the Hour comes while one of you has a palm seedling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before it arrives, let him plant it.[26] The teaching on the end of time is meant to make believers more responsible in this world.

Notes

  1. Quran 7:187; see also 31:34 and 79:42–44.
  2. Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Gabriel from Umar) and Sahih al-Bukhari 50 (from Abu Hurayra). Al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 1, pp. 150 and 158, and Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 1, p. 114 (Shamela text).
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the hadith of the man who asked about the Hour.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 3688, Book of the Companions, report of Anas ibn Malik.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 6503, the report of Sahl ibn Sad on the two fingers. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 11, p. 347 (Shamela text); on the day equal to a thousand years, Quran 22:47.
  6. Sahih Muslim 8, the hadith of Gabriel, which includes the competition in tall buildings. Al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 1, pp. 150 and 158 (Shamela text).
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 59 (Book of Knowledge, trust and the Hour) and 80 (the removal of knowledge). Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 1, pp. 141 and 178 (Shamela text).
  8. Sahih Muslim 2901, the hadith of the ten signs (Book of Tribulations and Signs of the Hour). Al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 18, p. 27 (Shamela text).
  9. Quran 27:82; 18:94–99; 21:96; 6:158.
  10. Quran 43:61; 4:159.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 2222, Book of Sales, report of Abu Hurayra.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 3346, Book of the Prophets, report of Zaynab bint Jahsh.
  13. Sahih al-Bukhari 3439, the report of Ibn Umar on the Dajjal. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 477 (Shamela text).
  14. Sahih al-Bukhari 3337, the report of Ibn Umar that every prophet warned his people about the Dajjal. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 6, p. 370 (Shamela text).
  15. Sahih Muslim 809, the report on the opening verses of Surah al-Kahf (some narrations name the closing verses). Al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 6, p. 92 (Shamela text).
  16. Sahih Muslim 588, the supplication for refuge taught after the final testimony in prayer. Al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 5, pp. 85–87 (Shamela text).
  17. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi; the grading of the Mahdi reports varies by scholar.
  18. Ibn Khaldun, al-Muqaddimah, the section on the Mahdi.
  19. Ibn Taymiyya, Minhaj al-sunna, on the Mahdi reports.
  20. Moojan Momen, An Introduction to Shi'i Islam (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1985), on the occultation of the twelfth imam.
  21. Quran 2:255.
  22. Quran 21:28; 53:26.
  23. Quran 2:254; 74:48.
  24. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the hadith of the great intercession; for the praised station, Quran 17:79.
  25. Quran 21:47; 99:7–8.
  26. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Musnad, report of Anas ibn Malik; al-Bukhari, al-Adab al-Mufrad 479.
